note: Read from tree-sitter-kotlin's scanner.c, which is itself a copy of
tree-sitter-julia's. The memory is one stack pushed two bytes at a time -
`{delimiter, prefix_len}` - and the census read that as a `marks` stack whose
element is a kind and a count. This book claims the string family and the
nested block comment, the import dot and the primary-constructor
keyword. The last two arrived from the Provision roll: every branch of
them is gated on `valid_symbols`, which rung 1 had no way to ask, so the
roll carried their bytes and none of their permission. Asked at the seam
they are whole. Automatic-semicolon insertion is still out of the cohort -
it answers a zero-width token at a position it marks *before* the bytes it
reads, and that is a seam question this book does not yet put.
`interp`, `brace` and `ident` are marks the C does not keep, and that is not a
liberty: the C is not asked inside an interpolation because STRING_CONTENT is
not in `valid_symbols` there, and rung 1 has no parse table to say so. They
are the parser's own bracket stack, standing in for it, and they carry no
answer - every rule that touches them emits nothing.
`_by_delegation_hint` is claimed by nobody and needs no rule: kotlin's own
scanner never emits it. It is declared so that it *appears* in `valid_symbols`,
where the automatic-semicolon branch reads it as a flag for "we are in a
delegation context" - so it is not a token at all, and no rule here could
stand in for one. Its absence costs no structure.

rules.name: interpolated_identifier_ends
rules.note: `$foo` hands the identifier to the parser, so content resumes where word characters stop - which is a test on the bytes at the offset, the same shape as a heredoc tag test, and not a length remembered from before.

rules.name: excess_dollars_are_content
rules.note: scanner.c:140-147. In a `$$"…"` string exactly two dollars interpolate; a third is literal, and the C answers with the *first* one alone and re-reads the rest on the next ask.

rules.name: interpolation_expression_starts
rules.note: scanner.c:152-165. `${}` is refused outright rather than answered zero-width, so the guard says the braces may not be empty.

rules.name: interpolation_identifier_starts
rules.note: scanner.c:166-170. The answer is the dollars only; the identifier behind them is the parser's.

rules.name: lone_dollars_are_content
rules.note: scanner.c:173-179. Too few dollars, or a dollar followed by anything that cannot begin a name: all of them are literal.

rules.name: escaped_dollar_closes_string
rules.note: scanner.c:188-199, and the comment there calls it an edge case: `"aa\$"` consumes the backslash, the dollar and the quote as one STRING_END. It is not gated on the delimiter being single, so a triple-quoted string closes on it too - transcribed as the C decides it, not as Kotlin means it.

rules.name: triple_content
rules.note: scanner.c:208-233. One or two quotes inside a triple-quoted string are content and are answered together with whatever came before them; three end it. `\` is not an escape here, so it is ordinary content.

rules.name: triple_closes
rules.note: scanner.c:242-249: `if we see a bunch of quotes in a row, then we just go until they stop appearing`.

rules.name: string_opens_triple
rules.note: scanner.c:72-96. The leading dollars are the interpolation prefix and the mark carries how many; a string with none still interpolates on one, which is why the count floors at 1.

rules.name: multiline_comment
rules.note: scanner.c:269-323. Nested, so the extent is a balanced run rather than a pattern, and an unterminated one ends at end of input because the C decided to answer it rather than refuse.

rules.name: roll:import_dot
rules.note: scanner.c:851-881, whole. `scan_import_dot` marks the end before the dot, consumes it, then skips whitespace: if a newline was crossed and `import` follows, the answer is an automatic semicolon at the marked position instead, so the dot is refused. That refusal is the lookahead here. The semicolon itself is the ASI branch and still out of this cohort, so refusing hands the offset back rather than answering it wrongly.

rules.name: roll:primary_constructor_keyword
rules.note: scanner.c:903-916. Both halves of the guard are transcribed: the C enters under `valid_symbols[PRIMARY_CONSTRUCTOR_KEYWORD] && !valid_symbols[STRING_CONTENT]`, and that second clause is why this rule can sit in `ordered` behind the string phases without racing them. It `skip`s leading whitespace rather than consuming it, so group 1 is dropped and the token is the word alone, and it requires a non-word byte after - `constructors` is an identifier.
